newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks to make economic appointments Friday.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks to make economic appointments Friday.

text.p: President Bill Clinton aims to make some Cabinet announcements on Friday, chiefly in the economic area, but has not made his final decisions, a senior administration source said on Thursday.
The source, who declined to be identified, said there was a "good chance" Clinton would make some appointments at a news conference scheduled for 2 p.m. EST (1900 GMT) on Friday.
Asked if they would concern his economic team, the source replied: "That's what we're looking at."
"My sense is that we are close to rolling out most, if not all, of the economic team," said another source.
Since Clinton won re-election on Nov. 5, seven Cabinet members have said that they plan to depart, including the commerce and labour secretaries.
Two key economic advisers are also leaving: Laura Tyson, who heads the National Economic Council, and Joseph Stiglitz, chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers.
However, administration officials said Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and his deputy, Lawrence Summers, are expected to remain in their jobs.
Conventional wisdom has been that Tyson's NEC job would be split between her deputy, Gene Sperling, and Dan Tarullo, the White House pointman on international economic issues.

But the senior administration source said the White House now appeared to be moving away from that scenario, although he would not disclose who may get the job. He added that the president had not yet made his final decisions on the matter.
Stuart Eizenstat, the undersecretary of commerce and a top White House official under former President Jimmy Carter, has also been mentioned as a potential candidate.
Another key job is the chairman of the president's Council of Economic Advisers.
Alan Blinder, a former CEA member and vice chairman of the Federal Reserve Board, has been sounded out about returning to the White House, but is said to be reluctant to do so.

Blinder was seen arriving at the White House on Thursday for an appointment with the incoming chief of staff Erskine Bowles, who was himself hesitant to return to Washington but who ultimately could not refuse Clinton's request.
Blinder left his job at the Federal Reserve, one of the most influential economic posts in the country, in January to teach at Princeton University.

Congressman Bill Richardson, a New Mexico Democrat who has led a string of high-profile missions to rescue U.S. citizens detained abroad, was said to be a candidate to be commerce secretary or U.N. ambassador.

Officials said they thought Richardson, who is Hispanic, was more likely to head the Commerce Department, which the Republicans want to close. "I don't think that the Republicans would risk alienating the Hispanic community by going after Commerce if Bill Richardson is the secretary," said one.

Former Democratic Sen. Harris Wofford of Pennsylvania and White House aide Alexis Herman have been cited as candidates for labour secretary, but one administration source suggested on Thursday that neither may get the job.
Wofford was also seen at the White House on Thursday.
Separately, administration officials said that Clinton was expected to meet Attorney General Janet Reno by the end of the week and was expected to keep her at the Justice Department.

Clinton last week unveiled his foreign policy team as a group, and White House officials said at the time that he was likely to do so with his economic team, saying the "chemistry" among them was critical. But this effort also complicates the process and officials were reluctant to say definitively Clinton would make personnel announcements on Friday.

"He's been working hard on Cabinet-related personnel issues. He's been focusing principally on the economic team," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said at his daily briefing. "I expect he'll have some more to say on that tomorrow."
Clinton himself, asked during a White House event on drug control on Thursday whether he would have some announcements to make, was coy, saying only: "Oh, I might, I might."
